A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MultiTP study, retaining its multilingual trolley problems, six moral dimensions and 19-model evaluation. Their main text, equations, tables, figures and complete appendices support a reliable comparison.

before.justification: v2 reports original LLM evaluations, including misalignment rankings, language clustering, speaker-count correlations and paraphrase-consistency results in Section 5 and Appendix D.

after.justification: v5 retains those original evaluations and adds translation-quality results, option-order consistency, regional analyses and further model comparisons in Appendices D–E.

M1.justification: The vignette-generation procedure, token-forced completions, presentation of both option orders and preference computation remain unchanged. Section 3.2 now lists translation as a third adaptation, but translation into 107 languages was already part of v2.

E1.justification: The core 107-language trolley benchmark and six moral dimensions are unchanged. Translation-validation coverage expands from an unspecified manual check in several major languages to human assessment of 44 languages, including low-resource languages, and automatic back-translation checks across languages. The regional analyses reuse existing geographic coverage.

E2.justification: The same 19 LLMs participate in the overall alignment and language-sensitivity comparisons. Additional analyses use models already evaluated in v2; no new comparator or competing translation method is introduced.

E3.justification: v5 substantially extends the validation protocols: five-point human ratings of 25 translation pairs per response, 169 responses across 44 languages, and back-translation evaluation using embedding cosine similarity. It also introduces regional grouping and an option-order consistency metric. Existing benchmark settings and paraphrase protocols remain unchanged; presenting both option orders was already documented in v2.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained paraphrase and language-clustering analyses, v5 adds human and automatic translation validation, tests the relationship between misalignment and language sensitivity, examines regional preference differences, and quantifies option-order robustness. These address additional validity and robustness questions rather than merely relocating the earlier appendix.

E5.justification: The new translation audit reports per-language means, standard deviations and annotation counts in Table 7, and adds a Spearman correlation analysis. Existing fixed-seed information and Pearson p-value reporting are retained. Neither PDF comparison establishes an increase in repeated model runs.

E6.justification: The main rankings, Table 3 sensitivity scores, speaker-count correlations and paraphrase results are retained. New results include 88.6% of 44 audited languages scoring at least 3/5, a back-translation similarity histogram, and a misalignment–sensitivity correlation of 0.43 with p = 0.07. Table 13 adds option-order consistency ranging from 87.1% for GPT-3 to 99.5% for GPT-4o Mini. Regional plots and Table 14's Llama-family preference entries further expand the empirical record.

T1.justification: The preference-vector definitions, L2 misalignment metric and language-sensitivity formula are unchanged. Neither version supplies theoretical propositions or proofs, and the added empirical validation does not introduce substantive mathematical theory.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the same dataset contribution and principal findings: most evaluated LLMs align poorly with human trolley preferences, while alignment does not clearly favor high-resource languages. The added appendix evidence does not redefine these core claims.

C2.justification: v2 already cautioned against high-stakes deployment and treating trolley problems as comprehensive moral assessments. v5 adds an explicit descriptive-versus-normative distinction in Section 3.1 and the Ethics Statement: matching culturally specific human preferences may be undesirable, and alignment should avoid perpetuating harmful biases. It also interprets the new checks as supporting translation quality and option-order robustness.

D1.justification: v5 supplies translation-annotation instructions, task duration and cost, clarifies greedy decoding, and updates the advertised code/data repository from moralmachine to multiTP. Existing model identifiers, VRAM requirements and approximate API budget remain. The brief sentence about extracting binary choices through post-processing is removed, without evidence of a procedural change.

R1.justification: v5 adds supporting references on translation evaluation (Lavie; Goto), positional effects (Liu), and the risks of reflecting human preferences (Bommasani; Ethayarajh and Jurafsky; Santurkar). Section 2 and the central positioning relative to earlier moral-alignment benchmarks remain substantially unchanged.

P1.justification: Changes include localized language corrections, revised author/affiliation and header text, expanded prompt explanations, and renaming Appendix B. Reproducibility and ethics statements move after the references, while the earlier results appendix becomes Appendix E. The main section order and five-question narrative remain largely intact.

P2.justification: v5 substantially expands the displays with a translation-quality table and histogram, a combined misalignment/sensitivity table, option-consistency and Llama-preference tables, and three regional multipanel figures. Existing clustering plots and the world map are retained and renumbered; main-text figures are relocated, and several table headings and captions are refined.

improvement.justification: v5 strengthens the evidence for translation fidelity and option-order robustness, and clarifies why matching human preferences is not necessarily ethically desirable. These are useful improvements to validation and interpretation. Their impact is limited by the translation audit's partial coverage and several single-response languages; its stated standard-deviation range also conflicts with Table 7. The additions improve transparency without fully resolving the study's validation limitations.
